title: Software Isn’t Losing Its Head. It’s Growing Thousands.
subtitle: Essay · with film
summary: Why AI finally lets strategy firms codify the method and keep the thinking personal.

essay.text: In 1999, Harvard Business Review asked consulting firms a simple question: what’s your strategy for managing knowledge? Strategy firms answered with their people. Knowledge lived in experienced heads and moved through conversation. Today, the same firms answer with their AI, and they say it loudly: every launch promises the methodology, codified and on demand. What drops out of that answer is the thing clients actually pay for, which is how their people think.
That answer has taken two forms.

The first gives the software a fixed head: a branded dashboard or a bespoke client tool with one polished interface. It demos well, and it gets one thing right: it keeps people on the methodology. But it does that by sending everyone down the same path, every time. Strategists don’t all work the same way, and neither does the work. The same project can call for a diagram one week, a spreadsheet the next, and a write-up after that. A tool holding the firm’s information should let people organize their thinking in whatever form the moment needs. A fixed head offers one.

The second cuts the head off entirely. It wraps the firm’s knowledge in a connector and puts it behind a chat window. This is the “headless” future many expect to replace SaaS: no interface, only a prompt. It is flexible, cheap, and technically impressive. Then a strategist opens it, stares at the blinking cursor, and has no idea what to ask. A blank box isn’t an interface.
Both camps are impressive. Neither is very useful to the person doing the thinking.

The 1999 article is worth going back to. Its authors, Morten Hansen, Nitin Nohria, and Thomas Tierney, found two answers across the industry. Implementation firms codified knowledge into databases built for reuse. Strategy firms kept it in their people. The authors’ advice was to lean hard one way, roughly 80/20, and never straddle the two.

Strategy firms had good reason to lean toward people. One Bain partner described the firm’s library of past work as “a picture of a cake without giving out the recipe.” The documents showed what the answer had been, not how anyone reached it.

Today’s two camps are both codification bets with different front doors. The fixed head packages the methodology into a product. The chat window lets you talk to it. Both assume the hard part is getting knowledge to the strategist. In strategy work, the hard part is what the strategist does with it.

Strategy isn’t retrieval. Nobody walks into a growth problem knowing the answer and needing a faster way to type it. You find the answer by working through it: framing the question, weighing the trade-offs, and making the call. Clients don’t pay for the data. They pay for what an experienced person decides it means.

figure.alt: Three hairline diagrams: points gathered inside a frame, a balance weighing two options, and many lines converging on one point.
figure.caption: Strategy isn’t retrieval: frame the question, weigh the trade-offs, make the call.

essay.text: Yet our tools decide how that thinking happens. A slide forces a linear story. A spreadsheet forces a grid. A chat window forces prose, and asks you to state the question before you have figured out what it is. Each is the right constraint for some moments and the wrong one for most. We have spent decades bending how strategists think around the shape of their tools, and calling the result a deliverable.

Edward Tufte made a version of this case about PowerPoint more than twenty years ago. He argued that bullet points and low-resolution slides chop reasoning into fragments, and that the content should decide the format. His fix was rich paper handouts. He was right, and it never scaled, because nobody could hand-build a new format for every argument. Now a model can.

The same shift breaks the trade-off Hansen and his co-authors described. In 1999, codification needed armies of librarians and personalization needed partners on planes, so no firm could afford to excel at both. AI changes that math. The engine can be codified while the head stays personal.
One head is too rigid. No head is too empty. The answer is more heads.

Many-headed software keeps a single engine underneath: the firm’s data, frameworks, quality bar, and point of view. On top, it grows a new head for each person and each moment. The form follows the thinking. Every option stays open until the strategist decides what the work needs, and the head takes shape around that decision.

figure.alt: One engine at the centre, labelled data, frameworks, quality bar and point of view, with windows growing from it on drawn lines.
figure.caption: The answer is more heads: one engine, a new head for every person and every moment.

essay.text: Through MAIA’s development, I’ve learned that an AI platform is an exercise in translation: between what the technology can do and what a team actually needs. A head is that translation, made for one person at one moment.

The obvious objection is that generated interfaces will scatter the work. If everyone sees something different, what keeps the methodology intact? The answer is where the guardrails live. In a fixed head, they live in the screen, so following the method means following the path. In many-headed software, they live in the engine, with the frameworks and the quality bar. The method holds whatever the screen looks like, and the interface can be as flexible as the work requires. That flexibility is what makes creativity possible.

For strategy firms, that changes the question. It is no longer which tool to build. It is how well the firm has encoded what can be encoded, and whether it has built heads that draw out what can’t. The firms that answer it won’t ship tools that expire. They’ll ship methodology that compounds.

figure.alt: Two curves over time: tools rise and then fall away, while methodology keeps climbing.
figure.caption: Tools expire. Methodology compounds. An illustration, not data.

title: Challenges of Adapting a Rules Based Monetary Policy Approach to Crisis Intervention
subtitle: Paper · with Zuber Chawla
summary: Excerpts from the paper: its abstract, what worked, what went wrong, and the playbook it proposes.

essay.heading: Abstract
essay.text: The paper investigates the Federal Reserve’s response to COVID-19, tracing how rapid rate reductions, aggressive quantitative easing, and special credit facilities kept markets afloat but cultivated the most resilient inflation since the early 1980s. Drawing on empirical evidence, we highlight the challenges of adapting a rules based monetary policy approach to crisis intervention. In contrast to the Great Recession’s slower pace of stimulus, the pandemic response overshot toward excess. The analysis concludes with a feasible three-pronged crisis playbook: deliver liquidity quickly, coordinate with fiscal policy, and tie every intervention to transparent, data-linked exit criteria. The findings emphasize that there is no need to reinvent the wheel, rather the Federal Reserve needs to maintain public trust and limit mission creep.

figure.alt: Two seesaws, after 2008 and after 2020, with slow growth and inflation at the ends. After 2008 the stimulus is too light to level the beam; after 2020 it is so heavy the beam tips the other way.
figure.caption: How much stimulus, and what it did: too little, too slowly after 2008; too much, too fast after 2020. The aim is a level beam.

essay.heading: What worked
essay.text: The Federal Reserve’s response to the COVID-19 pandemic reflected a direct application of monetary policy tools designed to stabilize financial markets and support recovery. Following a sharp contraction in spending and a surge in unemployment early in 2020, the Fed implemented expansionary policies to prevent a prolonged recession. During this period, the FOMC relied on three primary tools: adjusting the federal funds rate, balance sheet policies, and forward guidance.

essay.heading: What went wrong
essay.text: These insights highlight critical refinements necessary for future monetary policy: prudent interpretation of traditional economic indicators, reliance on thoroughly revised economic data, and the provision of detailed and transparent forward guidance.

points.text: One notable limitation was the Fed’s dependence on conventional economic indicators, specifically the Sahm Rule, which typically identifies recessions by observing a 0.5 percentage-point increase or greater in the three-month moving average of the unemployment rate from its recent low. During the pandemic, unusual labor-market dynamics, characterized by large numbers of workers rapidly re-entering rather than leaving employment, compromised the reliability of this indicator.

Moreover, preliminary economic data significantly hindered effective policy formulation. Initial metrics regarding employment growth and consumer savings underwent notable subsequent revisions, substantially altering policymakers’ initial perceptions of economic conditions. For example, the personal saving rate, initially reported at 2.9%, was later revised upward to 4.9%, demonstrating how reliance on early, incomplete data can misguide essential monetary policy decisions.

Additionally, forward guidance faced challenges. Forward guidance generally aims to shape market expectations by providing clarity on future policy intentions. However, empirical analysis revealed that forward guidance during the pandemic was only effective in influencing market behavior when accompanied by explicit numerical projections, such as those provided in the SEP.

figure.alt: A timeline of recessions from 1960 to 2020, each marked as called by the Sahm Rule, with an open mark at 2024 where it fired and no recession came.
figure.caption: The Sahm Rule called every recession since 1960. In 2024 it fired, and no recession came. Recessions: NBER. The Sahm Rule: Congressional Research Service.

essay.heading: A playbook for the next crisis
essay.text: What, then, should the playbook be for the next economic crisis? The Great Recession demonstrated the dangers of relying too heavily on markets to correct themselves, while the pandemic revealed the risks of excessive government intervention. An appropriate framework should integrate three key lessons from these downturns.

points.text: First, liquidity needs to reach stressed areas swiftly, but support measures must include clear end dates to avoid shifting expectations.
Second, effective fiscal policies must be in place to allow monetary policy to remain focused on the dual mandate, rather than becoming a catch-all rescue method.

Third, transparency is essential. Clear forward guidance about the criteria for both expansionary and contractionary policy reduces moral hazard by reminding markets that support is conditional and temporary.

figure.alt: Three panels: liquidity with an end date, fiscal and monetary policy moving together, and an intervention tied to an exit threshold.
figure.caption: The playbook: deliver liquidity fast with clear end dates, coordinate with fiscal policy, and tie every intervention to its exit.

essay.text: Neither a hands-off approach nor heavy intervention provides a lasting solution.

The future of monetary policy lies somewhere in between, wherein the Federal Reserve acts swiftly in a crisis, tapers effectively afterward, and avoids unnecessary expansion of its role. This balanced approach upholds the dual mandate and protects the Fed’s credibility for future uncertain challenges.

title: Turning Turbulence into Opportunity with AI Personas
subtitle: Case study · Prophet
summary: Turning tariff turbulence into opportunity with AI personas and rapid creative testing

essay.heading: Challenge
essay.text: A heritage men’s and boys’ footwear brand in the sub-$100 comfort segment was shifting to a product- and brand-led model anchored by a reengineered line built on proprietary technology.

Tariffs and global price volatility were squeezing margins and pushing retail prices up, so Prophet was tasked with turning turbulence into a growth opportunity. AI-driven research and cited industry studies indicated that tariff-linked price increases make consumers more likely to switch shoe brands, elevating price as a deciding factor.
In response, we focused on new-to-brand acquisition by (1) identifying and bringing to life high-potential segments and (2) aligning creative and messaging to what those switchers value most.

essay.heading: Solution
essay.text: To rapidly brainstorm and test in an ever-evolving, uncertain environment, we paired Prophet craft with consumr.ai’s digital-twin platform. Together with the client team, we defined and prioritized acquisition personas, then brought them to life as digital twins using consumr.ai. We ran simulated focus groups with the twins to map needs, pain points, and triggers across the purchase journey. We used these signals to translate insights into decision drivers while flagging friction to reduce.

We then benchmarked some of the client’s existing creative assets against persona preferences and iterated quickly. Using agentic image-generation, we built refined creative mockups (headline/visual/offer combinations tailored to each persona) and re-tested to converge on winners. Working in tight loops with the client leadership team, we cross-checked AI-derived findings against retail realities to de-risk decisions and codified the learnings into a persona-driven creative framework that scales across paid and onsite.

essay.heading: Results
essay.text: Our footwear client now has a persona-driven acquisition playbook and an end-to-end creative system that extends from paid media to onsite experiences. Refined ads consistently outperformed legacy creative on engagement testing, and clearer messaging around the benefit of their proprietary technology, as well as the refined promise, improved relevance scores. A repeatable test-and-iterate model now enables the client team to quickly identify and scale what works.

After creating the digital twins, we launched a one-day rapid email test to identify the top-performing creative. This proof point demonstrates that our client is now equipped with a strategy that turns past constraints to continue to deliver tangible growth.

title: Driving TPRM revenue by decoding a niche audience at speed
subtitle: Case study · Prophet

essay.heading: Challenge
essay.text: Coming off a Series B with a new CEO, Supply Wisdom, an emerging TPRM SaaS company, set out to turn momentum into revenue growth. Its platform continuously monitors 300+ indicators across financial, cyber, operational, nth-party, and location risk, but market signals pointed to tighter budgets, reduced price elasticity, and longer enterprise buying cycles. In a category where decision-makers are notoriously hard to interview, growth hinged on two imperatives: (1) sharpen buyer and user insight and (2) unify the message so marketing, sales, and product tell one simple, defensible story that increases qualified lead volume and improves conversion.

essay.heading: Solution
essay.text: To overcome the research constraint, we paired Prophet craft with Aaru’s survey simulations, drawing on millions of underlying data points to surface reliable patterns quickly. We ran two coordinated studies totaling ~20,000 agentic respondents across buyer and user roles and translated the findings into a market-ready narrative.

Working in rapid iteration loops with the Supply Wisdom leadership team, we pressure-tested direction in working sessions and cross-checked AI-derived signals against market expectations and prior research to de-risk decisions.

We first identified pain points and focus areas for key buyers (Chief Risk Officer, Chief Compliance Officer, Chief Financial Officer) and users (analysts and TPRM champions). We then generated splash-page mockups and tested hundreds of imagery/copy combinations to see what truly resonates, converging on outcome-tied clarity and low perceived lift as the most persuasive themes.

essay.heading: Results
essay.text: Supply Wisdom is now equipped with a unified, adaptable message and creative framework that scales across web, paid, and sales enablement, built to reach key buyers and users, and accelerate conversion without sacrificing rigor or credibility.

The work aligned marketing, sales, and product on clear priorities and gave revenue teams assets that map to each stage of the funnel. Select hero imagery and layout patterns resonated strongly with Supply Wisdom’s CEO and CFO, and the message architecture was designed to increase qualified pipeline, lift stage-to-stage conversion, and improve win rate.
By pairing Prophet craft with Aaru’s simulations, Supply Wisdom is positioned not just to grow, but to set the pace in third-party risk management.

title: AI and Crypto: Same Story, Different Technology
subtitle: Essay

essay.heading: The Parallel
essay.text: Crypto and AI share a structural similarity that gets overlooked: in both cases, the underlying technology is real, but the value assigned to companies is driven largely by narrative, presentation, and trust rather than by what the technology actually does. Understanding how that played out in crypto offers a useful lens for evaluating AI companies today.

essay.heading: How Crypto Lost the Plot
essay.text: Three dynamics eroded crypto’s credibility:

points.text: Crypto’s core pitch was decentralization, removing the need to trust banks or institutions. But companies like FTX were deeply centralized, dependent on opaque decision-making by a small group. The ideology became a marketing layer that obscured what was actually happening operationally.
Exchanges made confident assertions about reserves, safety, and backing that were never independently audited. When reality diverged from the claims, the damage was catastrophic.
Blockchain was real technology. But most crypto companies weren’t solving real problems, they were applying the tech to extract value through artificial scarcity and narrative-driven demand.

figure.alt: A mesh of points joined by faint dotted links, the network as pitched, with every point wired by a solid line to one centre, the network as operated.
figure.caption: Ideology masking reality: decentralized in the pitch, centralized inside.

essay.heading: Why AI Faces the Same Pressures
essay.text: AI has something crypto never had: genuine, demonstrable utility. But the same structural vulnerabilities exist:

points.text: Companies can’t reveal what’s actually inside their tools without destroying their competitive advantage. So trust gets built the same way crypto built it, through marketing, UI polish, and storytelling rather than transparency.

Foundation models are essentially a commodity. Everyone is building on similar underlying models. The actual differentiation comes from the wrapper: the interface, the positioning, the narrative about what the tool does. That means the UI is the marketing, and aesthetic experience becomes the primary signal of value for most users.

If an AI tool claims to simulate customer behavior or generate strategic insight, how do you validate that? Companies run internal tests, tune results, and present favorable outcomes. There’s no external standard for what “good output” actually means, which makes it easy to tell a compelling story that’s hard to falsify.

figure.alt: Five interface windows, each wired down to one shared bar labelled foundation model.
figure.caption: The wrapper economy: the model is a commodity, and the UI is the marketing.

essay.heading: Lessons from Crypto for Evaluating AI Companies

points.text: If a company can’t show you independent validation of their results, not internal benchmarks and not cherry-picked case studies, treat their claims the same way you’d treat an unaudited crypto exchange. The burden of proof should be on them.

points.lead: Separate the technology from the business model.
points.text: AI is real and useful. But that doesn’t mean every company built on top of it is solving a real problem. Ask what the company does that the foundation model alone doesn’t, and whether that wrapper is genuinely valuable or just a story.

points.lead: Watch what the UI is doing.
points.text: A polished interface is a signal, but it can also be a distraction. If the primary value proposition is how good the tool looks to use, that’s worth scrutinizing. Substance and aesthetics can diverge significantly.

figure.alt: A tall dotted bar marked claimed, beside an independent ruler whose marker stops partway up, at what is verified.
figure.caption: Demand verifiable claims: independent validation, not internal benchmarks.
